extracted.intended_audience: educators, policymakers, and foresters interested in organizing or reforming forestry education and training
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for what constitutes a school of forestry, how its curriculum, faculty, facilities, admissions, and practical training should be organized. Draws on European 19th-century practice and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'school of forestry'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'school of forestry' ... signifies an organization for the purpose of giving instruction in regard to all that pertains to the growth of trees, especially in masses, and their management, including their natural history, their adaptation to the arts, and their influence upon human welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forestry regards the forest as a growth carefully provided for; all means are used to develop it according to its purpose. The passage emphasizes that forestry is both science and art and treats forest growth as a long-term, planned enterprise (measured by centuries) rather than accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary scope requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Forestry involves botany, meteorology, geology, mineralogy, mechanics, and a large range of studies; 'no sooner is the subject taken into consideration in its true character, than it is seen to be interwoven with a very large range of studies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula should include natural sciences, mathematics, economics, law, and technical subjects because forest work requires understanding plant biology, climate, soils, physics, and other allied disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on practical/technical instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical teaching and practical forestry must be provided — practical illustration and application of theoretical instruction are essential; schools should be in the immediate vicinity of forest districts where practical study can be illustrated and applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the academy moved to Neustadt-Eberswalde to be near forests; excursions to forests should be frequent. Lack of suitable woodland near a school was criticized as a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course length and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses of instruction extend from two years to two and a half, or five semesters, with tendency to protract; examples range from two years to four years depending on institution and country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific institutions: Neustadt-Eberswalde five semesters; Carlsruhe a four-year program for state forestry candidates (first two years preparatory, next two years special forest studies); Vienna three years; Schemnitz arranged for four years. Programs should match the intended depth and state requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum structure: Fundamental, Principal, Secondary sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: At Neustadt-Eberswalde branches are arranged in 'Fundamental Sciences', 'Principal Sciences', and 'Secondary Sciences' with a total of 2,648 hours of instruction: 50% fundamental, 37% principal, 13% secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breakdown: Fundamental (1,328 hours) includes natural sciences, mathematics, economical sciences; Principal (980 hours) relates especially to forests, cultivation, protection, technics, law, excursions; Secondary (340 hours) includes jurisprudence, road construction, shooting. Use this three-part model to balance broad scientific foundations, forest-specific training, and ancillary practical/legal skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental sciences content and hour allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental Sciences include: 1. Natural Sciences — chemistry (theoretic and applied), physics and meteorology, mineralogy and geognosy, botany and forest botany, plant anatomy, physiology and pathology, microscopy, zoology (forest insects) — 840 hours; 2. Mathematics — geodesy, interest and rent account, wood-measuring, surveying and leveling, plan-drawing — 440 hours; 3. Economical Sciences — public economy and finances — 48 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precise hour allocations (840/440/48) are the Neustadt-Eberswalde example showing a heavy investment in natural sciences and mathematics as preparation for specialized forestry study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty composition and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful schools employ specialists: multiple teachers of forest science, instructors in mathematics/physics/mechanics/meteorology, chemistry/mineralogy/geognosy, botany, zoology, jurisprudence; assistants such as a royal chief forest officer and a chemist as assistant teacher of geology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where practical, use university professors for fundamental sciences and appoint specially qualified professors for technical forestry. A diverse faculty including scientific, technical, and legal expertise is recommended; some institutions list specific counts (e.g., director + 4 professors + 2 assistants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional arrangement: independent academy vs university attachment vs agricultural union
rubrics_metrics.description: Forest schools may be (1) independent and situated within forests, (2) part of the general course of a university or polytechnic, or (3) united with agricultural schools; examples and prominent schools are cited for each class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: independent schools offer better practical facilities; university attachment is economical for fundamental sciences, offers better libraries, academic atmosphere, higher-paid professors, and stimulation from allied departments; agricultural unions integrate agriculture and forestry. The tendency (esp. central/southern Germany) favors university connection for high positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions and preparatory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission requirements vary: Carlsruhe requires gymnasium completion and age 17 (state candidates); Vienna ordinary pupils must present a certificate of gymnasium or similar, extraordinary pupils must reach 17 and have preparatory training; Swiss sub-forester institutes require applicants at least 18 and passing an examination in primary studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some programs let foreigners attend only part of the course; state students may be subject to intermediate examinations (e.g., after two years in Carlsruhe an exam in natural philosophy and mathematics) and a final exam to qualify for state service. Admission criteria should match the level of training and career pathway intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examinations, examining bodies, and certification for state service
rubrics_metrics.description: Examinations may be administered by professors for intermediate exams and by a board including forest directors, a legal expert, professors of agriculture and forest management, and mathematics professors for final exams. Passing qualifies candidates for positions in the state service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Carlsruhe — end of second year examined by polytechnic professors; final exam by forest directors and various professors. Certificates award eligibility for appointment to assistant positions and eventual state service roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-graduation assignment and career progression
rubrics_metrics.description: After passing all examinations, candidates are assigned to general district foresters as assistants to gain practical experience and are given a tract of forest to manage; after six to ten years (depending on vacancies) they may be promoted to general district forester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This apprenticeship model ensures practical mastery before higher appointments and should be built into program expectations and career pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional facilities and collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Aids to instruction include valuable collections, chemical and physiological laboratories with greenhouses, forest gardens, extensive plantations and nurseries, museums, cabinets in botany/zoology/mineralogy/geology, instruments for physics and geodesy, stations for experiments on woods and for meteorology, and libraries (e.g., 5,500 volumes at Hohenheim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust physical infrastructure (labs, experimental stations, specimen collections, meteorological stations) is cited repeatedly as essential for practical and scientific training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class size and enrolment governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Some institutes specify limits: 'The number of pupils shall not exceed thirty' (Swiss forest institutes); other examples show varying averages (Giessen ~15, Tharandt ~50, Miinden ~75).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear enrollment caps to preserve instructional quality, especially for hands-on fieldwork; size should align with available practical facilities and instructional staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescribed syllabus for short-term practical institutes (Swiss schedule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Swiss two-month forest institutes should embrace: 1) forest surveys, marking, measurement and estimation, forest roads, protection against avalanches/slides; 2) study of kinds of wood and injurious herbs for sub-foresters; 3) elementary soil study and relations between soils; 4) indispensable ideas of climatology and meteorology; 5) cultivation and management of forests; 6) information for sub-foresters concerning working of forests, forest police, protection, and book-keeping; 7) number of pupils not to exceed thirty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This numbered schedule is presented as a suggested model for shorter, practical training programs intended to produce sub-foresters and to supplement longer formal schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fieldwork frequency and structure of practical exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical work is delivered via frequent excursions and exercises: Giessen reports two excursions weekly and journeys of one or two weeks in summer; Neustadt-Eberswalde emphasizes daily practical illustration and frequent excursions; district schools have weekly or annual practical sessions culminating in public examinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, scheduled field excursions (weekly/biweekly and longer summer trips) are essential to illustrate lectures and teach silvicultural operations directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional intensity and expected student workload
rubrics_metrics.description: At Neustadt-Eberswalde total time allotted yields an average of 28.5 hours per week of lessons (4.9 hours per day), with nearly as much time expected for study, making almost ten hours of daily work for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forestry courses should set and communicate a high instructional intensity comparable to a college course; curriculum planners must account for significant independent study time in addition to lectures and fieldwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and intended outcomes of forestry schooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions aim 'to impart a thorough, practical, and professional education' to future owners or managers of estates, farmers and foresters in public or private service, and 'to enable them to become champions of progress' in business and administration of forests. Some schools prepare specifically for state forest service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should be explicit about whether they prepare candidates for state service, private management, or sub-forester roles, and align curriculum, practical training, and examinations to those career outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered education system and lower-grade instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are higher academies, subordinate schools (one-year courses), district forest schools, and common schools teaching horticulture and tree-planting. Examples include secondary schools at Weisswasser, Eulenberg, Lemberg; district schools in Sweden; and private elementary schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design an educational ladder: elementary instruction for broad civic tree-planting literacy; one-year/secondary courses for sub-foresters; multi-year academy courses for professional foresters and engineers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government policy, appointment of teachers, and financial arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: In Switzerland teachers of institutes are appointed by cantons subject to federal approval and paid from the general treasury. Vienna distinguishes ordinary pupils (eligible for state stipends) and extraordinary pupils (must pay tuition and cannot receive state stipends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State involvement can include appointment and funding of teachers, stipends for certain classes of students, and legal frameworks (e.g., Swiss federal law supervising forest police). Financial/policy design should consider access, stipend eligibility, and teacher oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to foreign students and international training links
rubrics_metrics.description: Many schools host foreign students (e.g., Tharandt more than half foreigners; Great Britain sends 5–10 pupils annually to Nancy to train for colonial forests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs may serve international students and should consider admission options for foreigners (full course, partial attendance), the role of external students (externes), and cross-border training needs.
